item.title: Family office to billionaire Narayana Murthy to double exposure in India
item.description: It is targeting annual returns of 16% to 18%, Deepak Padaki, president of Catamaran Ventures LLP said on the sidelines of Bloomberg's New Economy Forum ...
item.dc:creator: Bloomberg
item.content:encoded: By Siddhi Nayak The family office of tech billionaire Narayana Murthy plans to double its exposure to India over the next five years, looking to capitalize opportunities in precision manufacturing and artificial intelligence as it seeks to expand a portfolio spanning listed and privately-held companies. It is targeting annual returns of 16% to 18%, Deepak Padaki, president of Catamaran Ventures LLP said on the sidelines of Bloomberg’s New Economy Forum on Wednesday. Its strategy combines investments in public and private markets, with an emphasis on sectors where Indian businesses can build capabilities for global customers, he added. Catamaran, one of the country’s largest private investors, runs $1.4 billion for the Infosys Ltd. founder, who is also the father-in-law of former UK Prime Minister Rishi Sunak. The Bangalore-based firm has holdings in Elon Musk’s SpaceX and the National Stock Exchange of India Ltd. Artificial intelligence is a key area of interest for the firm, particularly companies in India that offer specialized services, solutions and capabilities to larger enterprise businesses worldwide. Rather than limiting its focus to developers of AI models, Catamaran, a growth stage investor, is tracking AI-based enterprise solution providers, Padaki said. The approach comes as companies globally race to expand AI capabilities, creating demand for computing infrastructure, data centers and services that support the development and deployment of the technology. India’s opportunity extends beyond developing its own AI models to supplying the expertise and infrastructure required by global players. Data centers are another area attracting attention as AI workloads increase demand for energy solutions, cooling, computing power and storage.  Catamaran also favors precision manufacturing, a sector that could benefit as companies diversify supply chains and seek specialized suppliers, Padaki said. For Indian businesses, the opportunity lies in moving into higher-value manufacturing and supplying components or products that meet global standards, he added.

item.title: Open-source AI models carry more cybersecurity risks: Anthropic executive
item.description: Ahead of its expected public listing, Anthropic is facing increasing competition in countries that are growing more concerned about a reliance on American AI technology ...
item.dc:creator: Bloomberg
item.content:encoded: By Mark Bergen and Tom Mackenzie Anthropic PBC’s top sales executive outside the US argued that open alternatives to its AI models carry “more risk” of cybersecurity incidents or other dangers.  “We need to be really careful with open-source on safety,” Guillaume Princen, Anthropic’s head of international, told Bloomberg TV at the International AI Summit in Dublin on Wednesday. “I can’t talk for open models. But by definition, there’s more risk with them.” Ahead of its expected public listing, Anthropic is facing increasing competition in countries that are growing more concerned about a reliance on American AI technology. Popular alternatives are open-weight artificial intelligence models, whose parameters are publicly shared, letting them be modified and run by users on their own hardware. Advocates say these models are cheaper than the tightly controlled, closed systems offered by Anthropic and OpenAI, and better for national sovereignty. France’s Mistral AI recently released an open-weight model as a sovereign option for Europe. A flurry of similar open models from China are gaining traction outside the country.  Anthropic has also stepped up its warnings about AI’s capabilities. Earlier this week, the company warned that small AI models could soon power a new kind of botnet that can self-replicate across small, internet-connected devices like a smart oven. Princen, who also leads Anthropic’s sales efforts for startups and “digital native” companies, said his concerns about open-weight models derive from Anthropic’s efforts to secure its own products. After high-profile AI hacks, Anthropic said it has put in additional safeguards to keep its models from malicious behavior.  The company has advocated for slowing down AI development until international standards and consistent evaluation are in place. Addressing Anthropic’s more expensive models, Princen, who joined from Stripe Inc. in 2025, said he tells businesses that paying for more capable models will eventually pay off. “Always be investing on the frontier,” he said. “Because six months, a year, two years from now, the cost of that use case will also be going down.” He said the company’s latest Claude model, Opus 5.5, is 40% cheaper than a prior version. Enterprises paying for Anthropic’s “frontier” models make up a “very large part of the business,” he added, without offering specifics.  Princen declined to comment on Anthropic’s IPO plans or how much it is spending to train its new models.

item.title: US oil, gas supplies to India fall 43% as West Asia imports rebound
item.description: Refiners say high freight costs, longer voyages and limited supplies of medium sour crude make US barrels less attractive than West Asian and Russian alternatives ...
item.dc:creator: S Dinakar
item.content:encoded: West Asian producers led by the UAE, Iraq and Saudi Arabia will continue to be India’s leading energy suppliers once the war ends and cannot be replaced by the United States, three senior refining officials told Business Standard, as US oil and gas supplies fell sharply in September from this year’s high in May. Indian imports of crude oil, liquefied natural gas (LNG) and liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) from the US declined 43 per cent in September to a combined 1.22 million tonnes from 2.13 million tonnes in August, marking the lowest level since April, according to ship-tracking data accessed by Business Standard. Despite the West Asia conflict disrupting India’s energy supplies since March and forcing Indian refiners to seek alternative sources, US oil and gas supplies fell marginally from September 2025. They also declined by more than half from a two-year high of 2.86 million tonnes in October 2025. In value terms, this translates into billions of dollars in reduced purchases. Imports of oil and gas from West Asia surged 67 per cent in September from August to 13.56 million tonnes, ship-tracking data accessed by Business Standard showed. October imports so far are close to 6 million tonnes and may exceed September’s purchases, according to projections by maritime intelligence agency Kpler. Gulf oil exports rebounded to roughly 16.5 million barrels per day (bpd) in September, near pre-war levels, despite only 60 per cent of those barrels crossing the Strait of Hormuz compared with 83 per cent before the war. Saudi Arabia, the UAE and Iraq adapted through pipelines, bypass ports and extensive ship-to-ship transfers, trade journal OilPrice said, citing a note by Standard Chartered. Iran’s ability to choke off regional oil exports has consequently weakened, it added. Senior officials from state-run refiners said that while Washington was urging New Delhi to increase energy imports, the government had not issued any instructions on where to buy crude, LPG or LNG from. Economics remained the key consideration, they said. Record freight rates and limited supplies of medium sour crude grades from the US — the grades most suited to India’s complex refineries — have made imports of light sweet premium US crude less attractive to Indian refiners compared with Russian oil, the officials said. Crude oil imports from the US in October declined by around 30 per cent to 91,000 bpd compared with the whole of September, according to Kpler. Hiring rates for Very Large Crude Carriers (VLCCs), which can carry around 2 million barrels of crude, have jumped more than 20-fold from pre-war levels to nearly $1.5 million a day from $50,000-$75,000 in early 2026, a shipbroker from Abu Dhabi told Business Standard. Transportation and insurance now constitute 20-25 per cent of the value of a crude consignment compared with less than 5 per cent before the war, two refining officials said.Trade agreement hiccupsThe sharp decline in crude imports comes even as India and the US face hurdles in concluding a bilateral trade agreement, where higher energy purchases are a key demand of US President Donald Trump.United States Trade Representative Jamieson Greer has said signing a deal was not “imminent” because of a “universe of items that are sticking points”. Trump’s energy agenda has focused on policies enabling higher US oil and gas production while urging Europe, India, China and other Asian economies to buy more US energy as part of bilateral trade agreements. The European Union has stepped up purchases, with the US supplying a majority of its LNG and diesel. China also concluded a long-term LNG import contract during President Xi Jinping’s visit to Washington this month. There has, however, been little progress in efforts by Indian state-run oil companies to conclude LNG or crude import deals with the US, with current purchases remaining “opportunistic”, a senior refining official said. Speaking at the Munich Security Conference this month, Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman said talks were still under way for an India-US trade deal. “Although we’d like to believe that both the sides have reached a plateau beyond which giving or taking might be very, very difficult. But maybe if there are room to operate from, both sides could do it,” she said. That room is slowly shrinking. Trump signed into law last month the Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, giving him the authority to impose tariffs of up to 100 per cent on countries, including India and China, that continue buying Russian oil and gas. Overall imports of US fossil fuels, excluding coal, exceeded 2 million tonnes three times in the past six months, with May supplies at 2.58 million tonnes, the second-highest in five years after 2.86 million tonnes in pre-war October 2025, Kpler data showed. But imports slowed considerably in September and October, the data showed. Besides high freight costs and travel times of more than 45 days from the US — with vessels detouring around the Horn of Africa to avoid Houthi attacks around the Suez Canal route — supplies of medium sour grades from West Asia have surged in recent weeks. That has benefited Indian refiners and reduced their need to buy from alternative sources.

item.title: Wholesale inflation hits series high of 11.39% in September on broad rise
item.description: India's wholesale inflation rose to a series high of 11.39 per cent in September as food, fuel and manufactured product prices hardened across the board ...
item.dc:creator: Auhona Mukherjee
item.content:encoded: The wholesale price inflation (WPI) rate based on the 2022-23 series rose to its highest level of 11.39 per cent in September from 9.92 per cent in August, driven by a broad-based pick-up in prices of food, fuel and manufactured goods, according to government data released on Wednesday. The all-commodities index rose to 112.5 in September from 110.8 in August. The Ministry of Commerce and Industry also released India’s goods output producer price index (PPI), which rose to 112.5 in September, taking the PPI inflation rate to 11.39 per cent from 9.81 per cent in August. Fuel and power inflation rose to 25.85 per cent in September from 22.93 per cent in August as crude petroleum and natural gas inflation surged to 57.32 per cent from 34.41 per cent. Coal and lignite inflation also rose to 9.31 per cent from 1.57 per cent, while mineral oil inflation moved up to 40.02 per cent from 38.48 per cent. Electricity inflation remained negative at 0.43 per cent, but the contraction in electricity prices eased from 1.73 per cent in August. The surge in fuel and power inflation comes after a period of moderation between May and August. This was primarily driven by the crude petroleum and natural gas category, where inflation eased from 61.51 per cent in May before seeing a sharp uptick in September. For primary articles, inflation rose to 8.67 per cent in September, the highest in the new series, from 7.76 per cent in August. Within the group, food inflation jumped to a 21-month high of 8.14 per cent from 5.67 per cent in August, while minerals inflation rose to 9.51 per cent from 8.24 per cent, which more than offset the moderation in non-food inflation to 10.28 per cent from 14.79 per cent in August. The rate for manufactured products, which carry a weight of 63.1 per cent, rose to 9.76 per cent from 8.37 per cent — the highest in the current 2022–23 series. Within manufactured products, textiles, wearing apparel, chemicals and chemical products, basic metals, and electrical equipment witnessed a hardening in prices during the month. There was also a significant rise in inflation for computer, electronic, and optical products, which rose to 4 per cent after contracting for several months. Among output PPI major groups, the indices for agriculture, forestry and fishing; mining and quarrying; manufactured products; and electricity stood at 118.7, 129.2, 111 and 92, respectively, in September, against 116.5, 122, 109.7 and 90.9 in August. The trial input PPI for manufacturing, published on an experimental basis since March, rose to 106.1 in September from 104.2 in August.
